title: Why do safe cars crumple?
hook: A car that crushes in a crash sounds weak. Stopping slower changes the force by how much?

knows: mass in kg and speed in m/s
doesNotKnow: impulse: force times time equals change in momentum

misconception: A car that crumples is a weaker car; a stiff car is safer.
objective: The learner can explain that a crash must remove a fixed momentum, so doubling the stopping time halves the average force.

claims.text: Average force times stopping time equals the change in momentum (impulse), so the bar's area is the momentum removed.
claims.source: Impulse-momentum theorem, F_avg dt = dp; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 9.

claims.text: A 1000 kg car at 15 m/s carries 15,000 kg m/s of momentum, all removed when it stops.
claims.source: p = m v = 1000 x 15 = 15,000 kg m/s; final momentum zero.

claims.text: Stopping in 0.10 s takes an average force of 150 kN; in 0.20 s, 75 kN (half).
At a steady force, stopping from 15 m/s in t seconds crushes 15 t / 2 metres: 0.75 m in 0.10 s, 1.50 m in 0.20 s (0.38 to 2.25 m across the slider).
claims.source: Constant deceleration from v: distance = v t / 2 = 7.5 t m. t = 0.05..0.30 s gives 0.375, 0.75, 1.125, 1.5, 1.875, 2.25 m. Computed in Demo.tsx crush(). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: v t / 2 for t = 0.05..0.30 s gives 0.375, 0.75, 1.125, 1.5, 1.875, 2.25 m (0.38 to 2.25 m); slider min 50, max 300 ms step 50.

claims.text: The lesson uses a steady (average) force; real crash forces rise and fall during the stop.
claims.source: Stated idealisation. Fact-check 2026-10-13: a real 15 m/s frontal crash with about 0.6 m of crush lasts about 2 d / v = 0.08 s. | Builder fix 2026-10-13 (pass 4): dropped 'crush less and stop faster'; now says real tests sit near the 0.1 s / 0.75 m case. Sources: nhtsa.gov 18th ESV crash-pulse paper; pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3503406 (56 km/h = 15.6 m/s frontal barrier, 0.5-0.9 m, ~80-120 ms). · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: Demo.tsx reveal: 'Steady-force model; real crash forces rise and fall.' Matches the claim. Real frontal crash pulses are non-rectangular (peaked) per the cited NHTSA ESV crash-pulse work (not re-opened this pass); the claim makes no number-bearing statement.

claims.text: A crumple zone protects by crushing, which lengthens the stopping time and so lowers the force on the car and the people in it.
claims.source: Standard account of crumple-zone design (e.g. Hewitt, Conceptual Physics, ch. 6, impulse and momentum; vehicle crashworthiness literature). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Standard impulse-momentum account; with occupants held to the car (belts) the push on them scales with deceleration, so doubling the stop time halves it. Idealised: real restraints let the occupant's stop lag the car's slightly, so 'the same time' is the model, not exact. Accepted as stated since the reveal frames it as a steady-force model.

claims.text: The car's weight is about 9.8 kN, so 150 kN is about 15.3 car-weights and 75 kN about 7.6.
claims.source: Weight = 1000 kg x 9.81 m/s^2 = 9810 N. 150,000 / 9810 = 15.29; 75,000 / 9810 = 7.65 (shown 7.6 by toFixed(1) in Demo.tsx carWeights(); 7.645 rounds to 7.6). Slider: 300 kN = 30.6, 100 kN = 10.2, 60 kN = 6.1, 50 kN = 5.1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: 1000 x 9.81 = 9810 N; 150000/9810 = 15.29 -> 15.3; 75000/9810 = 7.645 -> toFixed(1) shows 7.6 (matches Demo.tsx carWeights); slider values 30.6, 15.3, 10.2, 7.6, 6.1, 5.1. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: Own node: 1000 x 9.81 = 9810 N; carWeights() toFixed(1) gives 30.6, 15.3, 10.2, 7.6, 6.1, 5.1 for 0.05-0.30 s. Predict's 'about 10 kN' is consistent with 9.8 kN.

recall.question: Jumping down, you land with stiff legs and stop in 0.05 s, or bend your knees and stop in 0.25 s. How does the average force on you compare?
options: Bent knees: one fifth as much
Bent knees: five times as much
recall.why: The momentum to remove is the same; five times the stopping time means one fifth of the average force.
